verses.t: Mencius said, "One who fully develops his heart knows his nature. Knowing his nature, he knows Heaven. To preserve one's heart and nourish one's nature is the way to serve Heaven. To be of one mind whether one dies young or lives long, and to cultivate oneself while waiting for whatever comes, is the way to establish one's destiny."

Mencius said, "Everything is destined, but one should accept willingly only one's proper destiny. So one who understands destiny will not stand beneath a tottering wall. To die having fully walked one's Way is a proper destiny. To die in fetters is not a proper destiny."

Mencius said, "Seek it and you will get it; let it go and you will lose it. In this case seeking helps one to get, because what is sought lies within oneself. Seeking it has its proper way, and getting it depends on destiny. In this case seeking does not help one to get, because what is sought lies outside oneself."

Mencius said, "All the ten thousand things are complete within me. There is no greater joy than to turn back upon oneself and find oneself sincere. Strive to treat others as you would be treated, and nothing will bring you closer to benevolence."
Mencius said, "To act without understanding what one does, to practice something without examining it, to follow the Way all one's life without knowing it: this is the condition of the multitude."
Mencius said, "A person must not be without shame. The shame of being without shame is shamelessness indeed."

Mencius said, "Shame matters greatly to a person. Those who are clever at schemes and tricks have no use for shame. If one is not ashamed of being unlike other people, in what way will one ever be like them?"

Mencius said, "The worthy kings of old loved goodness and forgot their own power. How could the worthy scholars of old have been otherwise? They delighted in their Way and forgot the power of others. So unless kings and dukes showed them the utmost respect and observed every courtesy, they could not see them often. If they could not even see them often, how much less could they make them their subjects!"

Mencius said to Song Goujian, "Are you fond of traveling to persuade rulers? Let me tell you about such travels. If others understand you, be content; if others do not understand you, be content." "What must one do to be content in this way?" "Honor virtue and delight in righteousness, and you can be content. So a scholar in hardship does not lose righteousness, and in success does not depart from the Way. Because he does not lose righteousness in hardship, the scholar keeps hold of himself; because he does not depart from the Way in success, the people are not disappointed in him. When the men of old realized their aims, their blessings reached the people; when they did not realize their aims, they cultivated themselves and became known to the world. In hardship they made themselves good in solitude; in success they made the whole world good as well."
Mencius said, "Those who wait for a King Wen before they rise up are ordinary people. Outstanding scholars rise up even without a King Wen."
Mencius said, "If a man were given the wealth of the families of Han and Wei, and still looked upon himself as lacking, he would be far above other men."

Mencius said, "If the people are employed with a view to their own ease, they will not complain even when hard worked. If people are put to death with a view to preserving life, they will not resent the one who kills them, even as they die."

Mencius said, "The people under an overlord look elated and pleased; the people under a true king look broad and content. When he puts them to death they do not resent it; when he benefits them they do not think of it as his merit. The people move daily toward goodness without knowing who makes them do so. Wherever the gentleman passes, people are transformed; wherever he abides, there is a spiritual influence. Above and below, he flows together with Heaven and Earth. How can it be said that he merely patches things up a little?"

Mencius said, "Benevolent words do not penetrate people as deeply as a reputation for benevolence. Good government does not win the people as well as good teaching. The people fear good government, but they love good teaching. Good government wins the people's wealth; good teaching wins the people's hearts."

Mencius said, "What people can do without having learned it is their innate ability; what they know without having thought about it is their innate knowledge. There is no small child who does not know to love his parents, and when he grows up there is none who does not know to respect his elder brother. Loving one's parents is benevolence; respecting one's elders is righteousness. All that is needed is to extend these to the whole world."

Mencius said, "When Shun lived deep in the mountains, dwelling among trees and rocks and roaming with deer and boars, there was very little to distinguish him from the wild people of the deep mountains. But when he heard a single good word or saw a single good deed, it was like a river bursting its banks: it swept on in a flood that nothing could stop."
Mencius said, "Do not do what you would not do; do not desire what you would not desire. That is all."

Mencius said, "People who possess virtue, wisdom, skill, and knowledge have usually acquired them through adversity. It is the solitary minister and the son of a concubine who keep their hearts on guard against danger and think deeply about trouble, and so they come to understand."

Mencius said, "There are those who serve a ruler: they serve that ruler by pleasing him and winning his favor. There are ministers who bring peace to the altars of the state: they take their pleasure in bringing peace to the altars of the state. There are Heaven's people: only when they know their Way can be put into practice throughout the world do they put it into practice. And there are great men: they rectify themselves, and others are rectified."

Mencius said, "The gentleman has three joys, and being king of the world is not one of them. That his father and mother are both alive and his brothers are free from trouble is the first joy. That he has nothing to be ashamed of when he looks up to Heaven, nothing to blush for when he looks down on men, is the second joy. That he gets the finest talents in the world and teaches and nurtures them is the third joy. The gentleman has three joys, and being king of the world is not one of them."

Mencius said, "Wide territory and a numerous people are things the gentleman desires, but his joy does not lie in them. To stand in the center of the world and bring peace to the people within the four seas is something the gentleman delights in, but what belongs to his nature does not lie in it. What belongs to the gentleman's nature is not increased when he acts on a grand scale, nor diminished when he lives in hardship, because his portion is fixed. What belongs to the gentleman's nature is benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, rooted in his heart. They show in his complexion, shining in his face, filling his back, and spreading through his four limbs, so that his limbs make it understood without words."

Mencius said, "Bo Yi, fleeing from Zhou [the tyrant], lived on the shore of the Northern Sea. When he heard that King Wen had risen, he said, 'Why not go and join him? I have heard that the Lord of the West takes good care of the old.' The Grand Duke, fleeing from Zhou, lived on the shore of the Eastern Sea. When he heard that King Wen had risen, he said, 'Why not go and join him? I have heard that the Lord of the West takes good care of the old.' If there is anyone in the world who takes good care of the old, benevolent men will regard him as the one to turn to. On a homestead of five mu, if mulberry trees are planted beneath the walls and the women raise silkworms, the old will have enough silk to wear. With five hens and two sows, if their breeding seasons are not neglected, the old will not go without meat. If a man tills a field of a hundred mu, a family of eight mouths will not go hungry. When it is said that the Lord of the West took good care of the old, it means that he regulated the fields and homesteads, taught the people to plant trees and raise animals, and guided their wives and children so that they would care for their old. At fifty one cannot keep warm without silk; at seventy one cannot be satisfied without meat. Not to be warm and not to be satisfied is called being cold and hungry. Among the people of King Wen there were no old people who were cold and hungry. That is what was meant."

Mencius said, "Put the fields in good order and lighten the taxes, and the people can be made rich. Let them eat in due season and spend according to ritual, and their wealth will be more than they can use. The people cannot live without water and fire, yet if you knock on someone's door at dusk to ask for water or fire, no one will refuse you, because these are so plentiful. A sage governing the world would make beans and grain as plentiful as water and fire. When beans and grain are as plentiful as water and fire, how could any of the people be unbenevolent?"

Mencius said, "Confucius climbed the Eastern Mountain and Lu seemed small to him; he climbed Mount Tai and the whole world seemed small to him. So for one who has gazed upon the sea, other waters hardly count, and for one who has studied at the gate of a sage, other words hardly count. There is an art to looking at water: one must look at its billows. The sun and moon are bright, and their light shines into every crack. Flowing water is such that it does not go on until it has filled every hollow; the gentleman who sets his mind on the Way does not attain it until he has achieved a complete pattern."

Mencius said, "Whoever rises at cockcrow and works diligently at doing good is a follower of Shun. Whoever rises at cockcrow and works diligently for profit is a follower of Robber Zhi. If you want to know the difference between Shun and Zhi, it is nothing other than the gap between profit and goodness."

Mencius said, "Yangzi chose 'everyone for himself': if by plucking out a single hair he could benefit the whole world, he would not do it. Mozi loved everyone without distinction: if by rubbing himself bare from the crown of his head to his heels he could benefit the world, he would do it. Zimo held to the middle. Holding to the middle is closer to the mark, but holding to the middle without weighing circumstances is just like holding to one extreme. What I dislike in holding to one extreme is that it injures the Way: it takes up one thing and neglects a hundred others."

Mencius said, "The hungry find any food sweet, and the thirsty find any drink sweet. They have not got the true taste of food and drink, because hunger and thirst have injured it. Is it only the mouth and belly that are injured by hunger and thirst? The human heart can be injured in the same way. If a person can keep the injury of hunger and thirst from injuring his heart, he need not worry about falling short of others."
Mencius said, "Liuxia Hui would not have exchanged his integrity for the post of one of the three highest ministers."
Mencius said, "Undertaking something is like digging a well. If you dig nine ren deep and do not reach the spring, it is still an abandoned well."

Mencius said, "Yao and Shun had it by nature; Tang and Wu embodied it [through effort]; the five overlords borrowed it. But if one borrows something long enough and never returns it, how can anyone know that it is not one's own?"

Gongsun Chou said, "Yi Yin said, 'I will not stay close to one who does not follow [the right].' He banished Tai Jia to Tong, and the people were greatly pleased. When Tai Jia became worthy, he brought him back, and the people were greatly pleased. When a worthy man is a minister and his ruler is not worthy, may he then banish him?" Mencius said, "If he has the intention of Yi Yin, he may; if he does not have the intention of Yi Yin, it is usurpation."

Gongsun Chou said, "The Ode says, 'He does not eat the bread of idleness.' Why is it that the gentleman eats without ploughing?" Mencius said, "When a gentleman lives in a state and its ruler employs him, the state becomes peaceful, rich, honored, and glorious; when its young people follow him, they become filial, respectful to their elders, loyal, and trustworthy. Who does more to avoid 'eating the bread of idleness' than he?"

Prince Dian asked, "What is the business of a scholar?" Mencius said, "To elevate his aims." "What do you mean by elevating his aims?" "Simply benevolence and righteousness. To kill a single innocent person is not benevolent; to take what does not belong to one is not righteous. Where is one's dwelling? In benevolence. Where is one's road? In righteousness. To dwell in benevolence and follow righteousness: with that the business of a great man is complete."

Mencius said, "Chen Zhongzi would not accept the state of Qi if it were offered to him improperly, and everyone believes this of him. But this is only the righteousness of refusing a basket of rice and a bowl of soup. There is nothing greater in a person than his relations to kin, to ruler and subject, to superiors and inferiors, and he cast these aside. How can one credit him with the great on the strength of the small?"

Tao Ying asked, "When Shun was Son of Heaven and Gao Yao was his minister of justice, if the Blind Man [Shun's father] had killed someone, what would have happened?" Mencius said, "Gao Yao would simply have arrested him." "Then would Shun not have prevented it?" "How could Shun have prevented it? Gao Yao had received his authority [from a proper source]." "Then what would Shun have done?" "Shun regarded giving up the world as no more than throwing away a worn-out sandal. He would have secretly carried his father on his back and fled, and lived somewhere along the seashore, happy to the end of his days, joyfully forgetting the world."

Mencius went from Fan to Qi and saw the son of the king of Qi from a distance. He sighed and said, "One's position changes one's bearing, as nourishment changes one's body. How great a thing is one's position! Is he not, after all, a son of man like everyone else?" Mencius said, "The prince's palace, carriages and horses, and clothes are mostly the same as other people's, yet the prince looks like that because his position makes him so. How much more one who dwells in the broadest dwelling in the world! The ruler of Lu once went to Song and called out at the Dieze gate. The gatekeeper said, 'This is not our ruler; how is it that his voice is so like our ruler's?' There was no other reason than that their positions were alike."

Mencius said, "To feed someone without loving him is to treat him like a pig; to love him without respecting him is to keep him like a pet animal. Respect and reverence are there before any gift is presented. If there is respect and reverence without substance, a gentleman cannot be held by such empty forms."
Mencius said, "Our bodily form and appearance are our Heaven-given nature. Only a sage can give full expression to his bodily form."

King Xuan of Qi wanted to shorten the period of mourning. Gongsun Chou said, "Is it not better to have a year's mourning than to stop altogether?" Mencius said, "That is like someone twisting his elder brother's arm and your telling him, 'Gently, gently, for now.' You should simply teach him filial piety and brotherly respect." There was a prince whose mother had died, and his tutor asked on his behalf that he be allowed to mourn for several months. Gongsun Chou said, "What about a case like this?" Mencius said, "Here the prince wants to complete the mourning but cannot. Even adding a single day is better than stopping. What I spoke of before was a case where no one forbids it and yet one does not do it."

Mencius said, "There are five ways in which the gentleman teaches. Some he transforms as timely rain transforms the land; some he helps to perfect their virtue; some he helps to develop their talents; some he answers when they ask questions; and some he influences privately so that they cultivate themselves at a distance. These five are the ways in which the gentleman teaches."

Gongsun Chou said, "The Way is lofty indeed and beautiful, but it seems like climbing up to Heaven, as if it cannot be reached. Why not make it something people might hope to attain, so that they would strive for it daily?" Mencius said, "A master carpenter does not change or discard his plumb line for the sake of a clumsy workman. Yi did not alter his standard for drawing the bow for the sake of a clumsy archer. The gentleman draws the bow but does not release the arrow; it is as if the arrow were leaping forth. He stands in the middle of the Way, and those who are able follow him."

Mencius said, "When the Way prevails in the world, one's person follows the Way wherever it goes; when the Way does not prevail in the world, one gives up one's person for the Way. I have never heard of anyone making the Way follow other people."

Gongduzi said, "When Teng Geng was among your students, he seemed to be someone you should treat with courtesy, yet you did not answer his questions. Why?" Mencius said, "I do not answer anyone who asks questions presuming on his rank, presuming on his worth, presuming on his age, presuming on his services, or presuming on old acquaintance. Teng Geng was guilty of two of these."

Mencius said, "One who stops where he should not stop will stop anywhere. One who is stingy with those he should treat generously will be stingy with everyone. Those who advance too quickly retreat just as fast."

Mencius said, "The gentleman cherishes creatures but is not benevolent toward them [as toward people]; he is benevolent toward the people but does not feel for them as he does for his kin. He feels for his kin and is benevolent toward the people; he is benevolent toward the people and cherishes creatures."

Mencius said, "The wise know everything, but they give urgency to what is most pressing. The benevolent love everyone, but they make it their urgent business to be close to the worthy. Even the wisdom of Yao and Shun did not extend to everything, because they gave urgency to the first priorities. Even the benevolence of Yao and Shun did not extend to loving everyone equally, because they gave urgency to closeness with the worthy. To be unable to keep the three years' mourning, yet to scrutinize the rules for three months' and five months' mourning; to bolt one's rice and gulp one's soup, yet to ask about not tearing dried meat with one's teeth: this is called not knowing what is pressing."
